newsitem.title: USA: Caterpillar seen unaffected by labor board rulings.
newsitem.headline: Caterpillar seen unaffected by labor board rulings.

text.p: Caterpillar Inc's shareholders should feel little if any impact from a series of rulings against the heavy equipment company by the National Labor Relations Board, analysts said on Friday.

Even if the United Auto Workers (UAW) prevailed in every complaint brought against Caterpillar in relation to labor actions this decade, the monetary awards would hardly dent the bottom line of the company, which earned almost $1.0 billion in the first nine months of 1996.
The NLRB in Peoria said there are more than 200 cases pending against Caterpillar.
"They've got 190 million shares outstanding," said Alexander Blanton, an analyst at Ingalls & Snyder. "It would not be very noticeable," referring to the impact of any monetary awards.

In the latest in a string of rulings against Caterpillar, the NLRB found that the company illegally provided free food and T-shirts to workers that crossed the UAW's picket lines -- benefits not available to strikers during an 18-month job action that ended in December 1995.
On Monday, Peoria, Illinois-based Caterpillar released a statement blasting the ruling.

"This is further evidence that the NLRB is willing to go to ridiculous lengths to support the UAW's harassment tactics against Caterpillar," Wayne Zimmerman, a Caterpillar vice president, said in the statement.
Still, Caterpillar probably factored in potential adverse NLRB rulings before union workers went on strike for a first time in 1992, analysts said.
"I suspect that they did that before they decided to take the first strike," said J. Blair Brumley, an analyst at Dain Bosworth.
In fact, Caterpillar shares are up about 25 percent since the latest strike ended, as the company has continued to post record earnings, though shares were unchanged at 76-3/4 Friday.
Caterpillar and the UAW were both shut down until the end of the year and could not be reached for comment.
